text: About the book: F. Scott Fitzgerald (born 1896 in St. Paul, Minnesota) published The Great Gatsby on 10 April 1925 with Scribner's. It sold modestly in his lifetime and he died in 1940 thinking it forgotten; it became a classic after the Second World War, when a cheap Armed Services Edition went to soldiers and schools took it up. The famous first-edition cover, a face over a night sky, was painted by Francis Cugat before the book was finished. Fitzgerald set the story in the summer of 1922 on Long Island, in the fictional towns of West Egg and East Egg.

Reading notes: the novel has nine chapters and runs about 47,000 words, so a chapter is twenty to thirty minutes of reading. The narrator is Nick Carraway, who tells the story a couple of years after the summer it describes. Good book-club pacing is one chapter per meeting for the first four, then two at a time. The text is free on Project Gutenberg and there are free LibriVox recordings.

Threads to watch without spoiling anything: how money is talked about (inherited money in East Egg, new money in West Egg, no money across the water); what Nick sees versus what he admits; the gap between how people present themselves and what they actually do; the past, and whether anyone can get it back; the small objects the book keeps returning to, such as lights, cars, clocks and eyes. A good question for any chapter: whom does Nick judge here, and does he judge himself?

Chapter 1: Nick Carraway, from a comfortable Midwestern family, has come east in 1922 to learn the bond business and rents a small house in West Egg, Long Island, next to a huge mansion owned by a Mr. Gatsby. He dines across the bay in fashionable East Egg with his cousin Daisy Buchanan, her powerful, restless husband Tom and the golfer Jordan Baker. Tom is called to the phone during dinner; Jordan says it is a woman in New York. Daisy talks brightly and says she has grown cynical. Back home Nick sees Gatsby alone on his lawn, stretching his arms toward a single green light across the water.

Chapter 2: Between West Egg and New York lies the valley of ashes, an industrial wasteland watched over by a faded billboard of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg's enormous eyes. Tom takes Nick to a garage there and introduces him to George Wilson, the owner, and to Wilson's wife Myrtle, who is Tom's mistress. In the city Myrtle buys a dog and hosts a drunken party in the apartment Tom keeps for her, with her sister Catherine and the McKees. When Myrtle keeps saying Daisy's name, Tom breaks her nose. Nick ends the night half-drunk, waiting for a train.

Chapter 3: Nick receives a formal invitation, delivered by Gatsby's chauffeur, to one of the lavish parties next door, where most guests were never invited at all. Rumors fly: Gatsby killed a man, Gatsby was a German spy. In the library a drunk man in owl-eyed glasses is astonished that the books are real. Nick talks for a while with a pleasant stranger about the war before realizing it is Gatsby himself, whose smile Nick finds rare and reassuring. Gatsby takes Jordan aside for a private talk she won't explain. Nick describes his working life in the city, his growing friendship with Jordan, her casual dishonesty, and calls himself one of the few honest people he knows.

Chapter 4: Nick lists the people who came to Gatsby's parties that summer. Gatsby drives him to New York in his huge cream-colored car and tells an unlikely life story (an Oxford education, war medals, rich Midwestern parents), then shows a medal and a photograph to prove it; a policeman who stops them waves them on after seeing a card. At lunch Nick meets Meyer Wolfsheim, a gambler said to have fixed the 1919 World Series, who wears cuff buttons made of human molars. Later Jordan tells Nick what Gatsby told her: in Louisville in 1917 Daisy loved a young officer named Gatsby; she married Tom in 1919 after a tearful night with a letter; Gatsby bought his house to be across the bay from her and wants Nick to invite Daisy to tea.

Chapter 5: Gatsby, anxious to repay Nick, offers him a vague business side-line, which Nick declines. On a rainy afternoon Daisy comes to Nick's house for tea; Gatsby, white with nerves, nearly flees, knocks a clock off the mantel and catches it. Nick leaves them alone and returns to find them changed, Daisy's face wet with tears. Gatsby shows them through his mansion, throwing his piles of shirts onto a table until Daisy cries at how beautiful they are. He mentions the green light at the end of her dock, and Nick senses it has just lost some of its magic by becoming real. Klipspringer, a house guest, is made to play the piano.

Chapter 6: A reporter turns up asking about Gatsby, and Nick tells the real story he learned later: Gatsby was born James Gatz to poor farmers in North Dakota, renamed himself at seventeen, and spent five years on the yacht of a rich miner, Dan Cody, who left him an inheritance he never received. Tom and the Sloanes stop by on horseback and casually snub Gatsby. Tom and Daisy attend a party; Daisy is unhappy there, and Tom decides Gatsby must be a bootlegger. Gatsby tells Nick he wants Daisy to say she never loved Tom, and insists the past can be repeated. He remembers kissing Daisy five years before.

Chapter 7: Gatsby ends his parties and fires his servants to keep Daisy's visits private. On the hottest day of the summer Nick and Gatsby lunch at the Buchanans', meet Daisy's small daughter, and Gatsby says Daisy's voice is full of money. The party drives to town; Tom insists on driving Gatsby's yellow car and stops for gas at Wilson's garage, where Wilson, sick and suspicious, says he plans to take Myrtle west. In a suite at the Plaza Hotel Tom confronts Gatsby, exposing his bootlegging with Wolfsheim, and Daisy draws back toward Tom. Driving home, the yellow car strikes and kills Myrtle, who ran into the road; it does not stop. Gatsby admits Daisy was driving. He keeps watch outside the Buchanans' house while Nick sees Tom and Daisy talking quietly in the kitchen.

Chapter 8: Before dawn Nick goes to Gatsby, who finally tells him about Louisville, Daisy's wealth and the letter he wrote her from Oxford. Nick leaves for work saying Gatsby is worth the whole rotten crowd put together, the only compliment he ever paid him. Through Michaelis, Wilson's neighbor, we follow Wilson's night: grief turning to certainty that the driver of the yellow car was Myrtle's lover, and that the eyes of Eckleburg are God's. Wilson walks to West Egg. Gatsby, waiting for a call from Daisy that never comes, floats in his pool on its first use of the summer; Wilson shoots him and then himself. Nick finds the body.

Chapter 9: Two years on, Nick remembers the aftermath. Reporters swarm; Daisy and Tom leave without a message; Wolfsheim declines to come. Gatsby's father Henry Gatz arrives from Minnesota, proud of his son, carrying a boyhood book with a self-improvement schedule written inside. Almost no one attends the funeral but Nick, the father and the owl-eyed man. Nick ends things with Jordan, then meets Tom on Fifth Avenue and learns Tom told Wilson whose car it was; Nick shakes his hand anyway, judging Tom and Daisy careless people who smash things and retreat into their money. He decides to go home to the Midwest. On the last night he looks at the Sound, imagines the Dutch sailors seeing the green new world, and ends with boats beating on against the current.

Who's who so far (from chapter 1): Nick Carraway, the narrator, a Midwesterner newly in the bond business, living in West Egg. Daisy Buchanan, his second cousin, charming and restless. Tom Buchanan, her husband, a rich former football star, physically imposing and quick to assert himself. Jordan Baker, Daisy's friend, a well-known golfer with a cool, bored manner. Jay Gatsby, Nick's neighbor, so far only a name and a figure on a lawn.

Who's who added in chapter 2: George Wilson, who runs a failing garage in the valley of ashes, worn and faintly handsome. Myrtle Wilson, his wife, vital and ambitious, Tom's mistress. Catherine, Myrtle's sister. Mr. and Mrs. McKee, the photographer and his wife from the apartment downstairs. Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, not a person but a pair of giant painted eyes on an old billboard.

Who's who added by chapter 4: Jay Gatsby himself, a courteous host with a remarkable smile and a shifting past he tells in pieces. Meyer Wolfsheim, a middle-aged gambler and businessman with ties to the 1919 World Series fix. The owl-eyed man, a party guest who marvels that Gatsby's books are real. Klipspringer, a boarder who seems to live at the mansion.

Open questions that work for any chapter: Which detail stayed with you, and why? Who is performing for whom in this chapter? What does Nick leave out or soften? Where does money show up when nobody is talking about it? Has your opinion of any character changed since the last chapter?
